claims.subject: tamil_tolkappiyam_base
claims.summary: Zvelebil reports that Agastya/Akattiyam is absent from the Tolkāppiyam base text and its prefatory stanza; Agastya appears in later commentary traditions.
claims.note: This distinguishes the grammar from its commentaries; it is not a claim that every manuscript or recension has been exhaustively collated.

claims.subject: tolkappiyar
claims.summary: Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar’s commentary on the Tolkāppiyam preface identifies Tolkāppiyar as Tiraṇatūmākkiṉi, son of Camata(k)kiṉi, and a pupil of Akattiyar.
claims.speaker: Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar as reported by Zvelebil
claims.note: The attribution belongs to the commentator’s account, not to an explicit statement in the Tolkāppiyam base text.

claims.subject: peraciriyar
claims.summary: Pērāciriyar acknowledges a view that Tolkāppiyar followed other now-lost grammatical works, then argues that he was Akattiyar’s foremost pupil and followed his teaching.
claims.speaker: Pērāciriyar as reported by Zvelebil
claims.note: Reports a debate among commentators and scholars; it does not establish a historical teacher-pupil relationship.

claims.subject: peraciriyar
claims.summary: Zvelebil reports Pērāciriyar’s attribution to Akattiyan of Tamil’s three divisions: iyal, icai, and nāṭakam; he also describes Akattiyam as the foundational text for Tolkāppiyam.
claims.speaker: Pērāciriyar as reported by Zvelebil
claims.note: These are statements attributed to the commentary, not surviving contents of a complete Akattiyam.

claims.subject: tamil
claims.summary: In canto 1, the sage Agastya tells the named Chola king Chembiyan Cheralāthan to hold an Indra festival at Pukār; the king agrees and invites Indra for twenty-eight days.
claims.speaker: Narrator
claims.note: A named Agastya appearance in the translated base poem; the narrated setting supplies no historical date for the sage.

claims.subject: tamil_manimekalai
claims.locator: Prologue, lines 00-10–00-20 (Tamil text); Hart explanatory prose, lines 202–203
claims.summary: The prologue narrates that Agastya’s karakam (water vessel) was overturned and the Kāviri emerged from its water.
claims.speaker: Narrator
claims.note: The Tamil passage and Hart’s translation do not name a crow in these verses. Hart’s surrounding explanatory prose says a crow turned the pot over; that detail is retained as translator-provided narrative explanation, not a direct verse claim.

claims.subject: tamil_kanthan
claims.summary: King Kānthan says he will seek the sage Agastya’s grace to resolve his troubles.
claims.speaker: King Kānthan in quoted speech
claims.note: The episode names Agastya inside the narrative; it does not date the episode historically.

claims.subject: velir
claims.summary: Kapilar’s poem praises a Vēḷ chief as descended through forty-nine generations from a lineage said to arise from an unnamed northern sage’s vessel and rule Tuvarai.
claims.speaker: Kapilar in the poem, as translated by Mahadevan
claims.note: The poem calls the figure only a “northern sage”; it does not name Agastya. The forty-nine generations refer to the Vēḷ lineage, not to the sage’s lifespan. Mahadevan’s equation of the sage with Agastya remains a separate identity hypothesis in the core graph.

claims.subject: naccinarkkiniyar
claims.summary: Mahadevan reports that Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar’s Tolkāppiyam commentary has Akattiyar lead eighteen Vēḷir families, eighteen kings, and Aruvaḷar from Tuvarāpati south, with Potiyil as his eventual abode.
claims.speaker: Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar as reported by Mahadevan
claims.note: This is a commentary narrative reported by a modern scholar. Tuvarāpati = Dvārakā is an identification, and the story supplies no verified migration date.

claims.subject: viracoliyam
claims.summary: Mahadevan reports the Tamil Buddhist tradition represented by Buddhamitra’s Vīracōḻiyam as making Avalokiteśvara the source from whom Agastya learned Tamil.
claims.speaker: Buddhist Tamil tradition as reported by Mahadevan
claims.note: The Vīracōḻiyam passage itself was not checked in an accessible translation here; this remains a report about a textual tradition.

findings: A pupil relationship with Akattiyar is a commentarial tradition attributed particularly to Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar and defended by Pērāciriyar; Zvelebil says neither the Tolkāppiyam base text nor its prefatory stanza names Agastya.
open_questions: Collate Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar’s and Pērāciriyar’s Tamil commentary passages directly against reliable editions and variants.

findings: Zvelebil reports that his Tolkāppiyam preface commentary names Tolkāppiyar as an Akattiyar pupil; Mahadevan reports a separate southern-migration narrative in the commentary.
open_questions: Check the actual Tamil commentary text and distinguish its wording from later editorial summaries.

findings: Zvelebil reports that he defended Akattiyar’s foundational role and Tolkāppiyar’s pupil status against an alternative account.
open_questions: Verify the cited Poruḷatikāram commentary passages in a reliable Tamil edition.

findings: In Puṟanāṉūṟu 201’s translated wording, Kapilar refers to a northern sage but does not name Agastya.
open_questions: Compare the poem’s Tamil text and old commentary with multiple translations; keep Agastya as an identification hypothesis.

findings: Mahadevan reports a Buddhist Tamil tradition in the Vīracōḻiyam associated with Avalokiteśvara teaching Tamil to Agastya.
open_questions: Locate and translate the relevant Vīracōḻiyam passage; do not infer the wording from the scholarly summary alone.

findings: Mahadevan reports a Tamil tradition in which Śiva teaches Tamil to Agastya.
open_questions: Identify and inspect the specific primary witness or witnesses and their date; this pass found no translation-checked passage.

findings: Mahadevan reports Skanda as an alternative Tamil teacher of Agastya.
open_questions: Identify and inspect the specific primary witness or witnesses; this pass found no translation-checked passage.

findings: Puṟanāṉūṟu 201’s translated passage ties a Vēḷ lineage to a northern sage’s vessel and forty-nine generations; Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar’s migration account is separately reported as leading Vēḷir groups south.
open_questions: Check the Old Tamil poem and commentary directly; keep the poem’s unnamed sage separate from the named Agastya of the commentary tradition.

findings: In Maṇimēkalai’s prologue, King Kānthan asks Kāviri to make his lineage flourish; in canto 22 he says he will seek Agastya’s grace.
Maṇimēkalai canto 1 names Chembiyan Cheralāthan as the Chola king whom Agastya instructs to hold Indra’s festival.
Puṟanāṉūṟu 201’s checked translation says “northern sage” but does not name Agastya.
open_questions: Compare the Old Tamil text and commentary directly; retain any Agastya equation as a hypothesis.
